"Francois Bernier, a French physician and philosopher who spent twelve years in India (1656–1668), addressed an influential letter to Jean-Baptiste Colbert, the French Minister of Finance under Louis XIV. As the ground is seldom tilled otherwise than by compulsion, and as no person is interested in sustaining the productivity of the soil, the country is neglected, agriculture falls to decay, and the peasantry is impoverished. questionText:

"Ibn Battuta was fascinated by plants that were completely unfamiliar to his North African audience. Describing the coconut, he wrote: 'These trees are among the most peculiar trees in the world... The nut of a coconut tree resembles a human head, for in it are what look like two eyes and a mouth, and inside, when it is green, there is what looks like brains, and within it which is like hair. Describing the betel (paan), he noted: 'The betel is a tree which is cultivated in the same manner as the grape-vine... The betel has no fruit and is grown only for the sake of its leaves... "Al-Biruni tried to explain the caste system by looking for parallels in other societies. In ancient Persia, he noted four classes: knights and princes; monks and fire-priests; lawyers, physicians, astronomers and other scientists; and peasants and artisans. In other words, he attempted to suggest that social divisions were not unique to India. At the same time, Al-Biruni disapproved of the Brahmanical notion of pollution. The sun cleanses the air, and the salt in the sea prevents the water from becoming foul. If it were not so, insisted Al-Biruni, life on earth would have been impossible.
